data.title: Prurigo nodularis — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Prurigo nodularis** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. What is prurigo nodularis (PN)? (PYQ)**
- Chronic, intensely itchy, firm hyperkeratotic nodules (few mm–2 cm) due to chronic scratching; the nodular type of 'chronic prurigo' (itch >6 weeks + scratch lesions)
- Middle-aged and elderly; symmetrical on extensor limbs, upper back (spares mid-back — 'butterfly sign'), buttocks

**Q2. Aetiological associations — work-up for a cause.**
- Dermatological: atopic dermatitis (most common association, 'atopic PN'), xerosis, insect bites, contact dermatitis
- Systemic: chronic kidney disease, liver disease (cholestasis, hepatitis C), diabetes, thyroid disease, iron deficiency, HIV, lymphoma/malignancy, gluten enteropathy
- Neurological: small fibre neuropathy, notalgia paraesthetica
- Psychiatric: depression, anxiety, OCD, substance use

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Neuroimmune circuit: itch–scratch cycle, increased dermal nerve fibres with reduced intraepidermal nerve density, neuropeptides (substance P, CGRP), IL-31, IL-4/13 (Th2), mast cells, eosinophils, periostin and fibrosis

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Marked hyperkeratosis, irregular/pseudoepitheliomatous acanthosis, fibrosis with vertical collagen, thickened dermal nerves (neural hyperplasia), increased mast cells and eosinophils

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Hypertrophic lichen planus, nodular scabies, insect-bite reactions, pemphigoid nodularis, multiple keratoacanthomas, perforating disorders (acquired reactive perforating collagenosis in diabetics/CKD), dermatitis artefacta, lichen amyloidosis, nodular prurigo of pregnancy, epidermolysis bullosa pruriginosa

**Q6. Investigations (screen for systemic disease).**
- CBC with eosinophils, renal and liver function, thyroid, blood sugar/HbA1c, iron studies, HIV, hepatitis B/C, chest X-ray, total IgE; biopsy (± DIF to exclude pemphigoid nodularis), skin scraping for scabies; age-appropriate cancer screening if indicated

**Q7. Management (step-wise).**
- Break the cycle: emollients, cooling lotions (menthol, polidocanol), keep nails short, occlude lesions
- Topical: super-potent steroid under occlusion, intralesional triamcinolone, calcipotriol, tacrolimus, capsaicin
- Phototherapy: NB-UVB, UVA1, PUVA; cryotherapy for individual nodules
- Systemic: gabapentin/pregabalin, antidepressants (paroxetine, mirtazapine, amitriptyline), naltrexone/opioid modulators, methotrexate, cyclosporine, thalidomide (neuropathy risk)
- Biologics: dupilumab (approved for PN), nemolizumab (anti-IL-31RA; approved for PN 2024); JAK inhibitors under study

**Q8. What is the butterfly sign?**
- Sparing of the mid-upper back (area patient cannot reach) — indicates lesions are from scratching

**Q9. Prognosis?**
- Very chronic; nodules persist months–years even after itch control; severe impact on sleep and mood

## Quick spotter facts
- Symmetric itchy hyperkeratotic nodules sparing mid-back — prurigo nodularis
- Screen kidney, liver, thyroid, HIV, malignancy

## Note
Nemolizumab approval for PN is newer than the textbooks — confirm current Indian availability.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Prurigo); EADV prurigo task-force concept of chronic prurigo. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
